tip: 'Depuis' wants the present, not the past: 'elle le connaît depuis longtemps' = she has known him a long time. Started back then and still true? French stays in present tense.
After a preposition, 'te' turns into 'toi': 'c'est pour toi', never 'pour te'. Once a word like 'pour' or 'avec' comes first, French switches to the strong form.
The '-s' on 'appelés' is doing grammar: when a direct object ('les') sits before 'avoir', the participle agrees with it; 'les' = them (masc.), so 'appelé' gains an 's'.
Two pronouns stack in a fixed order before the verb: 'leur en', never 'en leur'. Here 'leur' = to them and 'en' = about it: 'je leur en ai parlé'.
'Lui' means both "to him" and "to her" – one word covers either gender, and it parks in front of the verb: 'lui parle', never 'parle à lui'.
'S'asseoir' is irregular: 'elles se sont assises'. The '-es' on 'assises' marks agreement with the feminine plural 'elles'.
Counting forces an 'en': 'tu en as combien' carries a "of them" that English drops – "how many do you have (of them)".
'Se promener' = to take a walk. In 'nous nous promenons', the first 'nous' is the subject and the second belongs to the verb.
In the passive, the participle agrees with the subject: 'construite' takes an '-e' because 'la maison' is feminine.
To agree is "put yourselves in agreement": 'se mettre d'accord'. 'Elles se sont mises d'accord' = they came to an agreement, literally placed themselves in accord.
Reflexive verbs build the past with 'être', and the participle agrees with the subject: 'elle s'est habillée' picks up an '-e' for 'elle'.
A negative command keeps the pronoun in front: 'ne les ouvre pas'. Flip to a positive order and it jumps behind with a hyphen: 'ouvre-les'.
'Chercher' already means "look for", so the "for" is built in – 'la' (her) is a plain direct object, never 'chercher pour'.
Positive commands tack pronouns on with hyphens, and 'me' turns into 'moi': 'donne-le-moi' – the thing ('le') first, the person ('moi') second.
French "resembles TO" someone: 'ressembler à'. So the pronoun is 'lui' (to him/her), not 'le': 'tu lui ressembles'.
No "will" required – French often uses the plain present for a set plan: 'je te rappelle ce soir' = I'll call you back tonight.
Object pronouns normally land BEFORE the verb: 'il me comprend' = he understands me, literally "he me understands".
English can drop "some", French can't: "do you eat often?" still needs 'en' standing in for it – 'tu en manges souvent ?'
Quirk: a preceding 'en' never makes the participle agree. 'Elle en a commandé cinq' stays 'commandé', no 's' – unlike 'les a commandés'.
'Les' replaces plural direct objects: 'nous les attendons' = we wait for them.
'Reprendre' at the table means take another helping; 'en' stands for the food: 'elle en a repris deux fois' = she had seconds twice.
'Terminer par' = to finish with. 'Par' introduces what comes at the end.
'Avoir besoin de' hides a 'de', so "need it" brings the it back as 'en': 'j'en ai besoin' = literally "I have need OF it".
You phone TO someone in French: 'téléphoner à quelqu'un'. That 'à' becomes 'lui' – 'tu lui téléphones', not 'tu la téléphones'.
'Leur' here is the pronoun "to them", not the possessive 'leurs' – so it never takes an 's': 'il leur a raconté une histoire', plural yet still 'leur'.
Double pronouns: 'le' comes before 'lui' or 'leur': 'je le lui ai déjà dit'.
Two object pronouns stack before the verb, 'me' then 'le', and 'le' shortens before a vowel: 'elle ne me l'a jamais dit'.
'Sortir' normally builds its past with 'être', not 'avoir', so the participle agrees with the subject: 'elle est sortie' – that 'e' marks "she".
See someone do something = 'voir' + a bare infinitive: 'je la vois partir'. 'La' is who you see, 'partir' is the action, no "to".
'Depuis' takes the present where English needs "have been": 'tu la regardes depuis cinq minutes' = you've been watching for five minutes.
